records.our_prose: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season salad green with a peppery, mustardy flavor. It is one of the quickest things you can grow, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks, and it handles frost and even grows through winter in mild areas. Its main quirk is that it bolts (sends up a flower stalk) very fast in heat and long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter when it does. So it grows best in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and in hot places it is a fall-to-spring crop. Sow a little every couple of weeks for a steady supply. It is easy and beginner-friendly; the main pest to watch is the flea beetle, which chews tiny holes in the leaves. There is also a wild kind of arugula that is slower to bolt and even more peppery.

records.our_prose: Arugula (Eruca sativa), also called salad rocket or roquette, is a fast, cool-season leafy green in the mustard family (Brassicaceae), grown for its tender, peppery leaves. It is one of the quickest crops in the garden, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month, and it germinates readily even in cool soil and tolerates frost, so it can be sown very early and overwinters in mild zones. Its defining habit is how fast it bolts: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days send it to seed quickly, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does, so the spring window is short, fall is the main crop, and in hot regions it is grown through the cool fall, winter, and spring. A separate wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta) is slower, more pungent, and far slower to bolt. Arugula is easy, succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and a strong first-season choice, though flea beetles are its signature pest.

records.our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a fast spring-and-fall succession green built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since arugula tolerates frost and even germinates in cool soil, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady supply. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries a continuous crop straight through, while in the warmer end of this band (zones 6 and 7) midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for the main fall crop. A late-summer sowing run into fall is the most reliable, and a final sowing under a row cover can overwinter for the earliest spring picking.
records.source_context: Gradually thin to 6-inch spacings using thinnings for salads. Make new plantings every 2 to 3 weeks for a continuous supply until about a month before your average first frost date.

records.our_prose: Across the warm arid inland Southwest (zone 8 here), arugula bridges a cold-ish winter and a hot summer with spring and fall crops. Hard midsummer heat bolts it, so the calendar pauses through summer, and the coldest midwinter weeks are a brief cold gap. Sow every 2 to 3 weeks in the spring and fall windows.

records.our_prose: Arugula is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows so fast and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since they sprout even in cold soil and the plants handle frost. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat keeps the seeds from sprouting well and makes the plants bolt.

records.our_prose: Arugula is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it germinates readily even in cool soil, often in 5 to 7 days, and tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost. Sow a little more thickly than the final stand and thin to taste, eating the thinnings. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since warm soil above about 80°F cuts germination and lengthening warm days bolt the crop.
